item.title: Mutual defence, intel sharing part of the Mecca defence pact: Reports
item.description: The agreement commits the three countries to mutual military assistance and cooperation in intelligence, defence production, logistics and counter-terrorism ...
item.dc:creator: Martand Mishra
item.content:encoded: The full text of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye and containing a mutual defence clause, was published on Wednesday by a United Kingdom-based digital news website, Middle East Eye, which reported that the Turkish government has submitted the pact to its Parliament for ratification. The pact, signed in August, establishes a new international defence alliance similar to Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, according to which an armed attack against one member state is considered an armed attack against all member states. The text of the agreement, obtained by the media outlet, does not identify any specific country or region as a threat, but emphasises that all participating countries will take the necessary measures to support one another in the event of an armed attack against their independence, sovereignty or territorial integrity. This 16-article agreement commits the three countries to mutual military assistance and cooperation in intelligence, defence production, logistics and counter-terrorism. “If the territorial integrity, sovereignty, or internationally recognised borders of any of the ‘Parties’ are threatened or endangered, the ‘Parties’ shall use all necessary means to eliminate such threat(s) or danger(s),” the first article of the treaty states.Article 2 of the treaty states that “an externally originating armed attack against any of the ‘Parties’ shall be considered an attack against all the ‘Parties’.”Intelligence-sharing and defence The three countries will deepen cooperation in defence, defence industry and security, strengthen ties between their armed forces and undertake joint activities to improve defence cooperation under Article 3. The participating countries will also hold regular consultations on international security and develop individual and joint measures to protect their national security and address threats under Article 4. Article 5 of the treaty states that countries will strengthen cooperation against terrorism in all its forms, including joint efforts at the operational level, to safeguard regional and international security. The agreement also refers to Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, which recognises the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence. Article 9 provides for intelligence-sharing through mutually agreed secure channels, subject to covering information security, data protection and confidentiality. Under Article 10, the three countries will provide logistical support to one another during peacetime, war and other emergencies, including the supply of weapons, ammunition, fuel, spare parts and other equipment and compatibility of support services. Despite provisions for extensive intelligence and information-sharing, Article 13 restricts the disclosure of classified information and documents obtained under the agreement to any state, company or individual outside the three signatories. Article 16 states that the agreement will remain in force indefinitely once the required ratification procedures are completed. However, a member cannot withdraw during the first 10 years after the agreement enters into force. After that, withdrawal requires written diplomatic notification to the other signatories at least three months in advance. The agreement allows amendments through consultations and unanimous agreement among the core parties.

item.title: Indonesia protests: Why students and civil groups are taking to streets?
item.description: Students protest across Indonesia over rising living costs, forest fires and corruption, putting President Prabowo Subianto under renewed public pressure.
item.dc:creator: Sarjna Rai
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of students took to the streets across Indonesia on Tuesday, October 20, putting President Prabowo Subianto under renewed pressure as he completed two years in office. Demonstrations in Jakarta and several other cities highlighted growing public anger over the government’s handling of economic hardship and the environmental crisis. According to Reuters, authorities deployed around 9,000 police officers in Jakarta to manage the demonstrations. Protests were also reported in the Indonesian cities of Yogyakarta, Bandung, Pekanbaru and Makassar, with clashes between demonstrators and police in Yogyakarta. Why did the students protest? The students took to streets primarily to protest rising living costs, devastating forest fires and alleged corruption. Students and civil society groups are demanding stronger action on issues that directly affect their livelihoods and future. According to Reuters, students from the University of Indonesia cited the forest fires and a sharp stock market decline, alongside the weakening rupiah, as signs of the economy’s vulnerability. Their key demands include: Lower living costs: Protesters are demanding measures to ease household financial pressures and improve access to essential services, including education and healthcareAction against forest fires: Demonstrators have called for the government to declare the fires a national disaster and hold companies responsible for environmental damage accountableAction against corruption: Protesters are demanding stronger action against corruption, collusion and nepotism, alongside greater protection for freedom of expression. The agitators also flagged concerns over President Prabowo’s spending priorities, particularly his flagship free meals programme, amid rising living costs. In June, students protested against a fuel price increase and called for a rethink of the scheme, citing concerns over the cost of government spending. Forest fires, toxic haze fuel public anger The forest fire crisis has emerged as a major trigger for the latest protests. Fires across parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua have generated toxic haze, disrupted transport and forced schools to close in affected areas. Smoke has also spread to neighbouring countries, including Singapore and Malaysia. The fires have been worsened by dry conditions associated with El Niño, while the burning of peatlands has made the crisis harder to contain. Environmental groups have also raised concerns about forest clearance for palm oil plantations and the need to hold companies accountable. A day before the protests, President Prabowo directed officials to intensify aerial firefighting operations and improve coordination among security forces, forestry authorities and local communities. Indonesian authorities are also investigating 98 reports linked to forest and land fires. Greenpeace Indonesia activists climbed Jakarta’s Welcome Monument on Tuesday and displayed a banner calling for action on the climate crisis and lower living costs, highlighting how environmental concerns and economic pressures have converged in the protests. Indonesia’s earlier protests In August 2026, demonstrators gathered to mark a year since the anti-government protests of 2025. The rallies were followed by unrest in Jakarta, where more than 300 people were detained, according to Reuters. Indonesia witnessed nationwide protests in 2025 after a motorcycle ride-hailing driver died after being struck by an armoured police vehicle during demonstrations in Jakarta. The unrest claimed additional lives and fuelled calls for police accountability. The latest demonstrations come as Prabowo’s approval rating faces pressure. Reuters reported that Prabowo’s approval rating fell to 44.5 per cent in October, down from 81.2 per cent in November 2025.

item.title: HDFC Bank probe finds senior executives leaked secrets to outsiders
item.description: HDFC identified the executives during an internal investigation that began after some leaders grew concerned about the possibility of information being leaked ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Anto Antony An internal probe by HDFC Bank Ltd. — India’s largest by market value — found evidence that two senior executives disclosed confidential business strategies and possible market-sensitive information to outsiders, according to people familiar with the matter. The executives oversee certain key businesses and functions at the bank, according to the people, who asked not to be named discussing confidential matters.  HDFC identified the executives during an internal investigation that began after some leaders grew concerned about the possibility of information being leaked, the people said. The probe is still underway as the bank continues to examine whether the information was misused, the people said. An HDFC Bank spokesperson acknowledged an internal review, but didn’t comment on its findings or the executives involved. “In line with our policies, an internal review into this matter is currently underway to gather and evaluate all relevant facts,” the spokesperson said by email. “Appropriate action will be taken based on the findings, once the review is complete.” The bank said it was committed to upholding the highest standards of ethics and governance and takes reports of potential violations seriously. The review comes at a sensitive moment for HDFC Bank, which has a market value of about $115 billion and has spent three decades cultivating a reputation for conservative management, strong internal controls and consistent profitability. The lender is preparing for its first outsider chief executive following boardroom disputes and management departures. Its share price has declined about 28% this year. The probe and its findings were reported to senior management, including some members of the board, earlier this year, the people said. Both executives have since been formally informed of the findings, and it wasn’t immediately clear what disciplinary action will be taken, the people said.  The findings add to the challenges confronting Anup Bagchi, a veteran of rival ICICI Group, who is set to become HDFC Bank’s chief executive on Oct. 27.  In recent months, internal divisions in HDFC have played out publicly. In March, then-chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned abruptly, citing differences between his personal values and certain practices at the bank. An independent legal review commissioned by the lender subsequently said his concerns were not substantiated. Bagchi’s appointment follows the surprise decision of Sashidhar Jagdishan, the incumbent chief executive, not to seek another term. Jagdishan is stepping down after six years at the helm.  Kaizad Bharucha, deputy managing director and one of the bank’s longest-serving executives, has also asked to leave at the end of December. Founded in 1994, as the country opened its financial sector to private competition, HDFC Bank grew into a preferred investment for international fund managers seeking exposure to India’s rising incomes and expanding consumer credit.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military

Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defence drone missions against Russia

Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 8:21 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Elon Musk last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.   Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.   Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defence drone missions against Russia.   Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week, according to the report, which added the two had also discussed the matter prior to the decision to throttle Starlink.

Reuters had reported exclusively that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House. Also Read

Tesla shareholders to vote on Musk's re-election, $158 bn pay on Dec 3

Ukraine suspects US restricting intelligence sharing on Russian Attacks

Putin proposes summit with Trump, Xi Jinping to discuss Ukraine deal

Elon Musk says he will gift SpaceX shares to 'every kid in America'

Diesel deal aimed to keep peace talks with Russia going, says Trump

Trump said last week he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access, while Musk said any limits on speed or Starship use were decided by the US military or the president.   Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskky's relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskky.   Zelenskky, who is in Oslo in a bid to repair US relations, said on Tuesday he discussed issues including "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored" with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday Washington had not pulled back Ukraine's ability to access Starling's satellite network, but signaled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
